result.summary: Fragment 1 is Proclus' summary of the lost epic Cypria, running from Zeus's plan for the Trojan war through the Judgement of Paris, Helen's abduction, the gathering of the Greek fleet and the first nine years of fighting. Fragment 2 reports a tradition about the authorship, and Fragment 3 quotes lines saying Zeus began the war to relieve the overburdened earth.

scenes.title: Zeus's plan and the Judgement
scenes.summary: Zeus plans the war with Themis. Strife disrupts the wedding feast of Peleus, and Alexandrus judges the goddesses, choosing Aphrodite.
scenes.stakes: Alexandrus's choice among the goddesses sets the Trojan war in motion.

scenes.title: Alexandrus takes Helen
scenes.summary: Alexandrus builds ships and warnings are given. He is hosted in Sparta, and Aphrodite brings him and Helen together. They sail away, a storm drives them to Sidon, and they reach Troy. Meanwhile Castor and Polydeuces fight Idas and Lynceus.
scenes.stakes: Menelaus loses his wife and treasure; Castor dies in the cattle raid.

scenes.title: Gathering the Greek leaders
scenes.summary: Iris tells Menelaus the news. He plans war with his brother and visits Nestor, who tells digressive tales. The leaders are gathered, Odysseus's feigned madness is exposed, and they meet at Aulis for the omen.
scenes.stakes: Odysseus risks being forced to join; the expedition needs its leaders.

scenes.title: Teuthrania and Iphigeneia
scenes.summary: The Greeks mistakenly sack Teuthrania, fight Telephus and are scattered by a storm. At the second muster Agamemnon offends Artemis, and Iphigeneia is nearly sacrificed but is rescued.
scenes.stakes: Iphigeneia faces sacrifice; the fleet is held back by Artemis's anger.

scenes.title: War at Troy begins
scenes.summary: The fleet reaches Tenedos and lands at Troy, where Protesilaus dies. Achilles raids the region and the quarrel over prizes follows. Zeus plans to relieve the Trojans.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks must establish a landing and keep the army together against Trojan resistance.

scenes.title: Authorship of the Cypria
scenes.summary: Tzetzes says Stasinus composed the poem, which many attribute to Homer as a dowry gift.

scenes.title: Zeus relieves the earth
scenes.summary: Zeus pities the overburdened earth and starts the Trojan war to thin out mankind.
scenes.stakes: Mankind faces death in great numbers.

notable_quotes.reason: Gives the Cypria's reason for the war: Zeus lightening the earth of men.

analysis.text: The Cypria presents the Trojan war as the working out of Zeus's plan, with human quarrels, love and pride as its means.
The Cypria is lost and survives mainly through Proclus' summary, which shows how the epic cycle filled in the story around Homer's Iliad.

legacy.text: The Judgement of Paris and the sacrifice of Iphigeneia became central subjects for later Greek tragedy, Roman poetry and European art.

fun_facts.text: Proclus' summary is the main source for the Cypria's plot; only a few lines of the poem survive.

language_notes.text: Proclus' Chrestomathia is a summary of the epic cycle; this fragment is his précis of the Cypria, not the poem's own verse.
Strife (Eris) was not invited to the wedding; she threw in a golden apple marked for the fairest, causing the dispute. The summary omits this.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, son of Priam. Helen was promised to him by Aphrodite as his reward.
Lacedaemon is the region of Sparta in the southern Peloponnese, ruled by Menelaus.
Castor and Polydeuces are the Dioscuri, Helen's brothers; Idas and Lynceus were their cousins. The cattle raid led to their feud.
'Every other day' means the brothers alternate between living and being dead, sharing one immortality between them.
Iris is the gods' messenger. What happened at his home is Helen's departure with Paris, which began the Trojan War.
Ilium is another name for Troy, the city Paris came from.
The omen: a serpent devoured a sparrow's nest of eight young and the mother, which Calchas read as ten years of war before Troy fell.
Teuthrania was in Mysia, in Asia Minor, not Troy; the Greeks landed there by mistake.
Telephus, king of Mysia, was wounded by Achilles' spear; an oracle said only the wounder could heal him, hence his cure.
The Tauri were a people of the Crimea (Taurica), where Iphigeneia became a priestess of Artemis in later tradition.
Philoctetes, an archer who held the bow of Heracles, is abandoned on Lemnos; the Greeks later fetch him because Troy cannot fall without him.
Protesilaus is traditionally the first Greek to leap ashore at Troy and the first to die, as prophesied.
Achaeans is another name for the Greeks, as are Hellenes and Danaans in Homeric poetry.
"Detaching Achilles from the Hellenic confederacy" means separating him from the allied Greek army, which leads to his wrath in the Iliad.
"Dowry" refers to a tradition that Homer gave the poem to Stasinus as a marriage portion for his daughter.
"The load of death might empty the world" means mass death would lighten the earth's burden of overpopulation.

context_notes.text: Themis is a Titan goddess of divine law and order. Zeus's plan, per the Cypria, was to relieve the overburdened earth by causing a great war.
Helenus and Cassandra are Alexandrus' siblings, both prophets. Aeneas is a Trojan prince, son of Aphrodite.
Sidon was a major Phoenician city on the Levantine coast. Hera opposed Alexandrus because he had rejected her in the contest.
Nestor, the aged king of Pylos, is famous in epic for long speeches recalling the past as examples.
Odysseus pretended madness by yoking a horse and ox to plough; Palamedes put infant Telemachus before the plough, and Odysseus swerved, proving he was sane.
Artemis was goddess of the hunt and wild animals, so boasting of surpassing her as a hunter was an offence.
Cycnus, a son of Poseidon, was invulnerable to weapons, so Achilles is said to have killed him by strangling.
Briseis and Chryseis are the captive women whose allocation leads to the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon in the Iliad.
The scholiast cites this passage on Iliad i. 5, "the plan of Zeus was fulfilled," to explain what plan Homer meant.

literary_notes.text: Alexandrus is 'lured' by the promise of Helen; his choice, made for personal gain, will bring ruin on Troy.
The secret night flight with stolen treasure anticipates the violent war that the theft of Helen will cause.
Nestor's tales of other heroes' fates interrupt the main plot, as in his Homeric speeches, and offer cautionary parallels.
The omen and Calchas's prophecy signal the war's length and outcome before it begins.
Agamemnon's boast of surpassing a goddess is overweening pride, which prompts divine punishment.
The sham marriage turns a joyful occasion into a death sentence, using deceit against Iphigeneia.
Zeus's plan to detach Achilles anticipates the wrath and quarrel that drive the Iliad.
The earth is pictured as a living creature weighed down by humanity, which moves Zeus to pity and action.
The brief, declarative close affirms divine purpose, framing the war as the fulfilment of Zeus's will.
